summary:

────────
[4/5] Those features also provide strong signals to detect toxic prompts! Because they are easy to compute, we obtain a low-latency system. Validation is done on Llama2 and Mistral, for which we obtain 224 features in total (7*32 layers); we then simply fit a linear classifier on top.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/GAjWiNkXYAAtgLV.png

title: Randall Balestriero (@randall_balestr) — thread (5 tweets)
summary:
[1/5] Learning by reconstruction ``easily'' provides eye-candy samples...but the learned representation's ability to solve perception tasks is often a letdown. We pinpoint that misalignement, measure it, and show how some denoising tasks (masking) sometimes help
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/GGybm8FWEAAlT6l.png
────────
[2/5] That misalignment emerges as the features most useful for reconstruction live in a different subspace of the data compared to the features most useful for perception. ``good looking'' reconstruction can thus be achieved without capturing the features that solve perception tasks
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/GGydYDGW4AAohc2.png
────────
[3/5] Recent advances (MAEs) have found a way to push performances through hard coded denoising tasks (masking). We prove on a toy theoretical setting that masking helps for many datasets while additive Gaussian noise (original DAEs) is provably useless at reducing that misalignment
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/GGydv34WoAAwDVp.jpg
────────
[4/5] Those results provide some first steps tying (denoising) autoencoders to perception tasks, and have emerged from an amazing collaboration with @ylecun !
We hope that our quality measure of noise distributions will help extend MAEs! (@endernewton @sainingxie)
Code coming soon :)
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/GGyi_ZwWAAIcd1n.png
────────
[5/5] As a bonus, our findings also explain why long training time is required to `````finally''''' capture the features useful for perception tasks as part of the representation. Our findings open new avenues to speed up training through new denoising tasks!
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/GGyj1X5XMAApVmh.png

────────
[2/4] Furthermore, Batch-Normalization which is known to force the DN partition to concentrate near the training samples ( prevents robustness to emerge! In fact, Grokking is all about understanding the DN partition migration dynamics...
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/GHWT7r_XUAEHxrI.png
────────
[3/4] And as opposed to previous findings around Grokking, our observations hold across architectures, training datasets, and optimization settings!!!
Huge congrats to my long-term collaborator @imtiazprio and @rbaraniuk !
────────
[4/4] If your partition regions are large around training samples, you automatically control for robustness as it forces the DN to be affine near training samples ( turns out that if you keep training long enough, this naturally emerges!

title: Randall Balestriero (@randall_balestr) — thread (4 tweets)
summary:
[1/4] Joint embeddings (JEPAs) and density estimation/generative models seem to be like oil and water. Yet, we prove how a good JEPA is also a good density estimator! And JEPAs achieve that without input space reconstruction, get p(x) from any pretrained model!
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/G2vYwmDWYAE0j9j.jpg
────────
[2/4] And because of that, we can use any well trained JEPA as a score function to do sampling! This is obviously a very first microscopic step. Thus far all the strong density estimation and generative capabilities are measured and validated in synthetic settings, but stay tuned!
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/G2vZEjwW4AATlYe.jpg
────────
[3/4] That intuition is: if you want your embedding to be Gaussian or uniform on the sphere, you can only do so by learning the input density, otherwise how do you know which part of the input space to contract or expand? We are just using the good old change of coordinates formula!
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/G2vY4aHXAAAp6lU.jpg
────────
[4/4] We finally have a better understanding on how non-contrastive methods *do* learn an energy function of your data, something that @ylecun has said over and over! Incredibly happy to have pushed that research with the amazing Nicolas Ballas, Mike Rabbat and of course Yann @metaai

- what distribution to impose on your embeddings
- how to do distribution matching in high-dim

title: Randall Balestriero (@randall_balestr)
summary:
It’s not really about Gaussian vs. Laplace. It’s that JEPA is the only modern representation-learning method that even has a provably optimal embedding distribution. And it isn’t a trivial “L2 implies Gaussian” story; most L2-based methods don’t get anything like this. The optimality comes from the downstream minimax, not an assumed prior.
That it ends up being an isotropic Gaussian rather than, e.g., a uniform hypersphere, is ... beautiful.
(I have a good use for this property in mind.)
Quoting @giffmana
Am i the only one to think that the LeJEPA proof that optimal embedding space is isotopic Gaussian is pretty tautological?
Had they chosen l1 instead of l2 for knn and lasso instead of OLS for probe, they would have proven that Laplace is the optimal embedding space shape.
To me it sounds like proving that if you want to plug something in in Switzerland, using the Swiss plug type is optimal. But I'm neither mathematician nor electrician lol.
Don't get me wrong, maybe the method is good, i haven't tried it, but just i don't think this proof says as much and as broadly as people talking about it make it sound.

title: Randall Balestriero (@randall_balestr)
summary:
.@ylecun’s new paper lays out a full theory for JEPAs and turns it into a practical method – LeJEPA
Together with @randall_balestr, they highlight 2 key ideas behind JEPAs:
- The "ideal" form of JEPA embeddings is an isotropic Gaussian
- A new SIGReg objective pushes the embeddings toward that ideal
LeJEPA = JEPA prediction loss + SIGReg loss
It's a cleaner, theoretically grounded version of JEPA with several advantages:
- only one hyperparameter to tune
- no teacher-student models, no stop-gradient
- no special schedules
- scales efficiently
- works out-of-the-box on many architectures and datasets
There’s a lot to learn here. A breakdown of the key details ↓

title: Randall Balestriero (@randall_balestr)
summary:
I think you missed the main ideas.
- The basic premise of JEPA is that training by reconstructio/prediction in input space is evil (or counterproductive). The details are almost always unpredictable. Hence prediction must take place in representation space, where unpredictable details are eliminated.
- The main issue with JEPA is how to prevent collapse (in the absence of reconstruction loss). There are two classes of methods:
(1) EMA: Using weights in target encoder that are an exponential moving average (EMA) of the weights in other encoder (I-JEPA, V-JEPA, DINO, BYOL).
(2) Infomax: Using a regularizer that attempts to maximize the information content of the representation (e.g. over a batch). There are two sets of methods for that:
(2a) sample-contrastive methods: that want to make each representation vector different from the others (Siamese nets, DrLIM, SimCLR, etc). They tend to not work well in high dimension, to require large batches, and hard negative mining
(2b) dimension-contrastive methods: that want to make each variable independent from the others (Barlow Twins, VICReg, SIGReg/ LeJEPA, MMCR, MCR2....)
Bottom line:
A. SSL by reconstruction/prediction doesn't work for high-dim, continuous, noisy data
B. EMA sucks: no loss function being minimized, requirement for weightmsharing....
C. Sample-contrastive informax doesn't scale to high dimension
D. My money is on dimension-contrastive methods like SIGReg/LeJEPA

title: Randall Balestriero (@randall_balestr)
summary:
If you like LLM-JEPA, you’d love Semantic Tube Prediction (STP), our follow-up research that removes the required two-view structure and incurs no additional cost. It’s based on the Geodesic hypothesis, where trajectories of hidden states should be confined within a tube centered on a straight line connecting the first and last tokens. Semantic Tube explicitly separates noise (the component perpendicular to the tube) from signal. By adding an STP loss term, we can directly compress noise and significantly improve the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), which translates to better accuracy and data efficiency. We show that we need only a randomly selected 1/16 of the data to achieve the same accuracy. Besides better SNR, we made 4 more predictions that follow if the Geodesic hypothesis is true, and all of them are validated by our experiments.
A special thanks to my co-authors, @ylecun and @randall_balestr, for the fantastic collaboration on this work.

[1/3] SIGReg for pretraining Video Foundation Models! Our LeVJEPA opens many doors...
- stable recipe with a simple loss (sigreg + prediction)

- open source + reproducible
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HQz5e2CWgAEACJy.jpg
Quoting @lukaskuhn77
A new Pareto frontier in video pretraining.
Excited to introduce LeVJEPA 🔥: a stable, efficient end-to-end pretraining method that matches V-JEPA 2 at up to 20x less pretraining compute!
No target encoder, no masked prediction, no stop-gradient or teacher-student schedule.
One encoder, trained with a single objective. 🧵
🎬 https://pbs.twimg.com/amplify_video_thumb/2093294057317388288/img/7s5GlcU2WRd35uEW.jpg | https://video.twimg.com/amplify_video/2093294057317388288/vid/avc1/320x320/BCg8zdGnHGg7RFRE.mp4?tag=29

────────
[3/3] And because we can reach high masking ratio, flops are reduced by 20x compared to standard VJEPA1/2 setups. You can even train your video model on a single gaming gpu (see paper for details). Huge congrats to @lukaskuhn77 @lucasmaes_ @ylecun et al.!

clean_title: H-JEPA: end-to-end learned hierarchical world models for visual planning
summary:
[1/4] Introducing H-JEPA: the first end-to-end learned hierarchical world model for long-horizon visual planning!
Built atop SIGReg/LeWM, H-JEPA provides a stable training recipe where semantic abstractions naturally emerge across levels...
Paper+Code: 🧵👇
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HT88Y42WgAA-1Ll.jpg
────────
[2/4] Training such a hierarchical JEPA **end-to-end** means that we need to prevent dimensional collapse... As you probably guessed, we leverage SIGReg to keep latent spaces well-conditioned across all levels without relying on complicated heuristics! It is stable and easy to debug!
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HT8849jXQAApJTN.jpg
────────
[3/4] Semantic abstraction yields temporal compression!
By forcing higher levels to discard fast-varying, unpredictable details, the representations naturally evolve on slower timescales. Hence, they can predict far ahead into the future--while lower levels handle local execution.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HT88zhvW8AATwJR.jpg
────────
[4/4] The benefits of hierarchy are now clearly showcased across experiments/environments, from simulations to the real world... but this won't come as a surprise if you followed @ylecun talks! This has been a huge work led by @kevinghstz, @BasileTerv987, Mike and @ylecun! Try it out!
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HT89io6WQAA5pgV.jpg
clean_summary:
When you want a model to plan visually over long horizons, it helps to build a hierarchy that captures different levels of detail. But training such a hierarchical model end-to-end is tricky because the latent spaces can collapse or become unstable.

Randall Balestriero presents H-JEPA, which uses SIGReg to keep latent spaces well-conditioned across levels without complex heuristics. This leads to semantic abstractions that evolve on slower timescales, letting higher levels predict far into the future while lower levels handle immediate details. Experiments show clear benefits across simulations and real-world tasks.

title: Randall Balestriero (@randall_balestr)
clean_title: DSReg recovers individual world latents without reconstruction
summary:
LeJEPA already identified the world's latents--up to some mixing. There is now a very simple post-training recipe to undo that ambiguity and to recover the disentangled world's features! What a time to be Gaussian :)
📄
Quoting @YujiaZheng9
Is it possible to provably recover individual latent variables of the true world, even without reconstruction (e.g., JEPA)?
Yes, with DSReg, a simple regularization that can be applied post hoc to your pretrained model!
🎬 https://pbs.twimg.com/amplify_video_thumb/2108262997827133440/img/GonRDaN6k2Cw21gs.jpg | https://video.twimg.com/amplify_video/2108262997827133440/vid/avc1/674x270/HHE1CRxSVhgAspbj.mp4?tag=29
clean_summary:
When models learn latent variables representing the world, they often mix these variables together, making it hard to identify each one separately. This mixing creates ambiguity, limiting how well we understand the underlying features.

Randall Balestriero highlights DSReg, a simple regularization method applied after training that can undo this mixing. DSReg provably recovers the disentangled latent variables without needing to reconstruct the original data. This means you can get clear, separate world features from a pretrained model, improving interpretability and analysis.
